short: Money a federal agency transfers to an outside body to carry out a public purpose set in law, without expecting to be closely involved in the work.
An award like a grant, except that the agency expects to be substantially involved in the work while it is carried out.
The instrument an agency uses to buy property or services for the Government's own use. It is not a grant, and this guide does not cover it.
The federal term for grants, cooperative agreements and other aid given to carry out a public purpose, as distinct from the Government buying something for itself.
A grant for which the agency selects the recipient, through a competition or on the merit of proposals, and decides the amount.
Federal money that a law divides among states, territories or local governments by a set formula, with no competition among applicants.
Federal money paid to a state, territory, tribe or local government, which then funds local providers. A non-profit applies to that government, not to the federal agency.
An organisation that receives a federal award and hands part of it on to another organisation as a subaward.
Part of a federal award that the recipient passes to another organisation to carry out part of the programme, with the federal terms attached.
An organisation that receives a subaward and carries out part of a federal programme, as distinct from a contractor that sells goods or services.
The state body that receives a federal formula or block grant and passes it on. A local organisation applies to it, not to the federal agency.
The formal public announcement that a federal agency has money to award under a programme, with the rules for applying.
NSF's name for a focused funding notice that runs for a limited period and sets its own rules on who may submit and how.
A standing, broad NIH notice through which an investigator sends in an application on a topic of the investigator's own choosing.
A standing notice, used by the defence research offices among others, that invites research proposals across the whole range of an office's interests.
A letter NSF publishes to give information, clarify policy or announce its interest in proposals or supplements on a topic.
The entry, with its number, that each federal assistance programme has in the public catalogue kept at SAM.gov.
The identifier an agency gives to one funding notice. It appears in the notice's summary on Grants.gov.
An agency's advance listing on Grants.gov of a notice it plans to publish, with estimated dates. It is not yet open for applications.
A short notice sent to a funder before the application, saying that one is coming. Some notices require it and others make it optional.
A short first-stage submission that a funder reads before the full application, to invite, encourage or discourage it.
A summary of a project idea, about two pages long, that NSF asks for before certain kinds of proposal so that a programme officer can judge fit.
A competition in which the funder caps how many applications one institution may send, so the institution chooses internally first.
The official document by which an agency makes an award. It states the amount, the dates, and the terms and conditions.

term: Budget period and period of performance
short: The period of performance is the whole span of an award, from start date to end date. It is divided into budget periods, each funded in turn.
Funding for the next budget period of an award already made, issued without a new competition.
An application to carry a funded project into a further project period. It competes again for the money.
An application sent again, in revised form, after an earlier version was not funded.
Extra money added to an award that is already running, asked for by the organisation that holds the award.
More time to finish a funded project: the end date of the award moves later, under rules the award sets.
The part of a project's cost that federal funds do not pay. Also called matching.

term: Community Project Funding and Congressionally Directed Spending
short: Money that Congress directs to a named recipient and project in an appropriations act. The House and the Senate each have a name for it.
The set of forms that make up one application to one funding notice, filled in and submitted through Grants.gov.
The government-wide rules for federal grants and cooperative agreements: how an award is administered, what costs it may pay and when the recipient is audited.
The numbered collection in which federal regulations are printed. A citation such as 2 CFR part 200 gives the title first and the part after it.
The publication in which federal rules, proposed rules, executive orders and agency notices appear, each with a citation of its own.
The part of the Uniform Guidance that decides what an award may pay for. A cost has to be allowable, and to be allowable it has to be reasonable and allocable.
A cost that an award is permitted to pay under the cost principles and the award's own terms.
Costs that can be tied to one particular award, such as the salaries and supplies of the project it funds.
Costs of running an organisation that serve many projects at once and cannot readily be assigned to one award. An award pays them as a percentage of its direct costs.
The document recording the indirect cost rate that one federal agency has negotiated with an organisation on behalf of all federal agencies.
A flat indirect cost rate that an organisation with no negotiated rate may charge without negotiating one with the government.
The base of direct costs to which an indirect cost rate is usually applied. It leaves out equipment and several other kinds of cost.
The one federal agency that reviews, negotiates and approves an organisation's indirect cost rate on behalf of all federal agencies.
A ceiling on the indirect cost rate an award will pay, set by statute, regulation or a funder's policy, whatever rate the organisation has negotiated.
The audit an organisation must have for any fiscal year in which its spending of federal awards reaches a set threshold.
The government site, run by GSA, where an organisation files its single audit and where anyone may search the audits that have been filed.
The ending of an award, in whole or in part, before the planned end of its period of performance.
The steps that finish an award after its period of performance ends: final reports, settling of obligations and the return of money not spent.
Written permission a recipient needs from the funding agency before it makes certain changes to a project or charges certain kinds of cost.
A ceiling on the rate of salary that grant funds may pay one person, set at Executive Level II of the federal pay scale.
A separate budget category that, in NSF's undergraduate research programme, holds student stipends, housing and travel. It is left out of the base for indirect costs.
The check a federal agency makes of an applicant's finances, systems and record before it makes an award. It can end in extra conditions on the award.
The standard federal application form, issued in several sets for different kinds of applicant and programme and filled in through Grants.gov.
The standard form on which a recipient reports to the agency on the money of an award, at intervals the award sets.
The government-wide standard format in which a recipient reports progress on a research award. Each agency collects it in its own system.
A document in an application that says what will be done with the data a project produces: where the data will be kept, and when others may use them.
Federal requirements on training, disclosure and institutional safeguards that attach to research funding. People certify training; large institutions certify a programme.
A disclosure by each senior person on an application of their sources of support, foreign ones included, made on a government-wide form.
A standard document about each senior person on an application, giving their appointments and affiliations. It is now a government-wide form prepared in SciENcv.
The federal rules for research that involves people. An institution files an assurance with the government, and a review board approves each study.
The document in which an institution describes its animal care programme and commits to federal policy on laboratory animals. It is needed before funded animal work starts.
A statement, required for larger awards, that the applicant has made no unallowable lobbying payments and will report non-federal funds used for lobbying.
NIH's governing policy guide for its grants. By accepting an award a recipient agrees to follow it unless the notice of award says otherwise.

term: Proposal and Award Policies and Procedures Guide (PAPPG)
short: NSF's governing guide to preparing a proposal and managing an award. NSF has proposed to replace it.
A presidential order of August 7, 2025 on how federal agencies decide on and manage discretionary grants, including review by a senior appointee.
The federal office that issues the government-wide rules for grants, the Uniform Guidance, which each grant-making agency then adopts.
The assessment of applications against criteria set out beforehand, usually by reviewers who know the field, before an agency decides what to fund.
At NIH, the committee of reviewers that gives an application its first level of peer review. NIH's formal name for it is scientific review group.
The body of an NIH institute that gives an application its second level of review and makes funding recommendations to the institute's director.
The NIH centre that receives grant applications and organises their first level of peer review in study sections.
The final score that NIH peer review reports for an application as a whole. NIH proposed in August 2026 to stop reporting it.
A figure that NIH reports from peer review together with an application's final overall impact score. NIH proposed in August 2026 to stop reporting it.
A cut-off in overall impact scores that an NIH institute used to settle which applications it would fund. NIH institutes no longer rely on paylines.
The document that gives an applicant the results of peer review of an application, at NIH and at AHRQ.
The two criteria, approved by the National Science Board, on which NSF judges every proposal.
The share of applications in a year that receive an award. A funding rate may count something else, such as applicants in place of applications.
A member of a funder's staff who looks after a field or a programme and is the person an applicant asks whether a project fits.
The agency official responsible for the business side of an award, as distinct from its science: review, negotiation, award and administration.
The person named in an application to lead the project and answer for the conduct of the work. NIH writes PD/PI, for program director/principal investigator.
The naming of two or more people to lead one project. NIH speaks of multiple PD/PIs; NSF names a PI and co-PIs.
The person an organisation authorises to submit applications on its behalf and to sign the certifications that go with them.
The office inside an applicant organisation that explains the application process and roles to its researchers and sets up their system accounts.
The legal body that submits an application and, if it succeeds, holds the award. In most federal research funding it is an institution and not a person.
An NIH standing for a lead investigator within 10 years of the final research degree or clinical training who has not yet won a substantial independent NIH research award.
A three-character code by which NIH labels each kind of award, such as R01, K08 or T32. The first character usually shows the funding category.
NIH's code for its research project grant: one defined project, led by a named investigator or investigators, for up to five years.
Two NIH codes for small grants of up to two years: the R21 for exploratory work and the R03 for small projects. Neither can be renewed.
NIH's code for research grants to institutions that have had little NIH support: AREA for undergraduate-focused ones, REAP for health professional and graduate schools.
NIH's code for a research project funded as a cooperative agreement, in which NIH staff take part in the work after the award is made.
NIH's code for a one-year grant that buys a research instrument for a group of NIH-funded investigators to share. It pays no indirect costs.
An NIH award that gives a named researcher salary and research support, with protected time, to develop a research career. The institution applies for the candidate.
An NIH fellowship for one named doctoral student or postdoctoral researcher, who trains under a sponsor. It pays a stipend and allowances, and no indirect costs.
An NIH grant to an institution to run a research training programme. The institution, not NIH, selects the trainees, who receive NRSA stipends.
The family of NIH research training awards, named for Ruth L. Kirschstein, that pay a stipend to a student or postdoctoral researcher on a fellowship or a training grant.
NSF's five-year award for untenured, tenure-track faculty who combine research and education. The employing organisation submits for one investigator.
An NSF fellowship that gives a graduate student three years of support for a research-based degree in a STEM field. The student applies directly to NSF.
Two NSF proposal types: EAGER for early exploratory work on untested ideas, RAPID for time-sensitive work. Each starts with a concept outline to the programme officer.
A fixed sum paid to a fellow or trainee to live on during training, at a level the funder sets.
A fixed yearly sum paid to the institution that hosts a fellow, for costs such as health insurance, supplies and administration. A fellowship that pays one often pays no indirect costs.
A condition of some training awards and scholarships: the recipient owes a period of qualifying work afterwards, or may have to repay the money.
A programme that pays down a person's educational debt in return for a period of qualifying work, such as research or teaching. The person applies, not the employer.
The identifier SAM.gov assigns to an organisation. Every federal application carries it, and a subrecipient needs one before a subaward can be made.
The federal registry, run by the General Services Administration, in which an organisation holds an active registration before it applies for federal grant money in its own name.
A Commercial and Government Entity code, given to a domestic organisation as part of its SAM.gov registration. A foreign organisation obtains an NCAGE code first.
The person an organisation names in its SAM.gov registration as its contact for electronic business. That person controls who may act for the organisation in Grants.gov.
The federal website where most agencies post funding opportunities and receive applications.
The shared space in Grants.gov where a team fills in the forms of one application package before an authorised person submits it.
The NIH-run system in which an applicant organisation and its people hold accounts for applications, awards and reports. Several other agencies use it as well.
The eRA module in which an application is prepared online, checked for errors and sent on through Grants.gov.
The National Science Foundation's own system for preparing and submitting proposals and for filing reports after an award.
NASA's system for grant proposals before award. The organisation and every person with a role in a proposal register in it.
The Department of Justice system in which the full grant application is submitted and awards are managed.
A web-based grants management system that some federal agencies use to issue and manage awards. Recipients see the Notice of Award in it and file requests and reports.
The Health Resources and Services Administration's own grants system. Some HRSA notices need a second submission in it after Grants.gov, and recipients file progress reports there.
The DOE Office of Science system in which letters of intent and pre-applications are submitted. The application itself goes through Grants.gov.
The portal of the Congressionally Directed Medical Research Programs, where the pre-application that every one of its funding opportunities requires is submitted.
The online system in which recipients of NEH and IMLS awards manage them after award: reports, requests for changes and messages to the agency.
The Department of Education's grants and financial management system, which replaced G5 in 2023. Grantees draw down payments in it.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency's grants management system, used to apply for, track and manage its grants.
The Department of Agriculture's online system for applying for and managing USDA grants and agreements.
The Department of Housing and Urban Development's electronic system for Continuum of Care applications and grants management.
A federal sign-in service that lets one personal account open many government websites, among them most of the grant systems.
A shared service of the Department of Health and Human Services that pays out grant funds for federal agencies. Recipients draw down money and file financial reports in it.
The Treasury system through which some federal agencies pay grant money to recipient organisations. The paying agency, not the recipient, starts the enrolment.
A persistent identifier for an individual researcher, free to the researcher. NIH requires one of every person who submits a Common Form.
A researcher profile system, run by NCBI at the National Library of Medicine, in which the federal biographical sketch and current and pending support forms are produced.
The interagency online system in which recipients of federal funding report inventions made under their awards to the funding agency.
The site on which the next generation of Grants.gov is being built. Its search became the default search for federal funding opportunities in December 2025.
The Internal Revenue Service's public look-up for tax-exempt organisations, where a funder checks a non-profit's standing and anyone can read its filed returns.
The federal biomedical research agency, part of the Department of Health and Human Services. Its institutes and centers fund research at universities, medical schools and other organisations.
One of the component bodies of NIH, each with its own research agenda. The institute or center that would pay for an award decides whether to fund it.
The federal agency that funds research and education across science and engineering, through grants, cooperative agreements and fellowships.
One of the eight large units of the National Science Foundation. Each covers a group of fields, runs its own programmes and posts its own funding opportunities.
The part of the Department of Energy that funds basic research in the physical sciences and related fields at universities, non-profits, firms and national laboratories.
A defence research and development agency that funds universities and others. Its programme managers define programmes and choose who performs the work.
A defence office that funds biomedical research in programmes named by Congress, with money Congress adds each year.
NASA's yearly omnibus call for research proposals in space and Earth science: one announcement holding many programme elements, each with its own scope and due dates.

term: National Institute of Food and Agriculture (NIFA)
short: The Department of Agriculture's agency for funding agricultural research, education and extension outside the department. AFRI is its largest competitive programme.
The federal agency that funds the humanities, with grants to colleges, museums, libraries, research institutions, independent scholars and other non-profits.
The federal agency that funds arts projects by organisations, and research on the value and impact of the arts.

term: Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS)
short: The federal agency that makes grants to museums, libraries and related organisations.
The statistics, research and evaluation arm of the Department of Education. Two of its centres run the department's education research grant competitions.

term: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA)
short: A Department of Health and Human Services agency that funds mental health and substance use services, training and capacity through block grants and discretionary grants.
A Department of Health and Human Services agency that is mainly a funder of health services and the health workforce, with a small research line in maternal and child health.
The Department of Health and Human Services agency for children, youth and family programmes, among them Head Start and block grants to states and tribes.
The Department of Health and Human Services agency that funds services for older adults and people with disabilities. NIDILRR is its disability research institute.

term: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
short: A Department of Health and Human Services agency that funds outside research through its centres and institutes, among them NIOSH, its institute for occupational safety and health.

term: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)
short: The Department of Health and Human Services agency for health services research: the quality, safety and delivery of health care.
An independent non-profit research funder, authorised by Congress, that pays for studies comparing how well clinical options work for patients. Its awards are contracts.
The federal national service agency. It funds organisations to engage members and volunteers in service.
An independent non-profit set up by Congress that passes its annual appropriation to local non-profit legal aid programmes.
HUD's yearly homeless assistance competition, and the local body through which projects enter it. A project goes into that body's single application and does not apply alone.
The Department of Justice's main grant-making office. Its bureaus fund reentry, victim services, juvenile justice and related programmes.

term: Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)
short: The federal department that holds NIH, CDC, HRSA, SAMHSA, ACF, ACL and AHRQ. Its grants policy statement covers its agencies other than NIH.
A college or university, as a class of applicant in federal grant notices. Notices list it apart from other non-profits, and some programmes are open to it alone.
A non-profit that the IRS has recognised as tax-exempt under section 501(c)(3). Federal notices and many foundations ask for this status by name.
A 501(c)(3) organisation that the IRS has not classed as a private foundation, such as a school, a hospital, a church or a body supported by the public.
An arrangement in which one organisation oversees the money side for a project or group that has no tax-exempt status of its own. Funders differ on whether they accept it.
A programme at NSF, with counterparts at other agencies, to raise the research competitiveness of listed states and territories. An institution qualifies by where it is.
NIH's programme to build biomedical research capacity in states that have had low levels of NIH funding. An institution qualifies by being in a listed state.
A college or university placed in a class defined by the students it enrols or by its history. Funders define the class in different ways, so the notice in hand decides.
A college or university founded before 1964 with the principal mission of educating Black Americans. The class is closed: statute and a list in regulation fix it.
A college that meets the Title V tests for an eligible institution and whose full-time-equivalent undergraduate enrolment is at least 25 percent Hispanic. The status follows enrolment.
A college that qualifies under one of the federal statutes on tribally controlled colleges, or is named among the 1994 land-grant institutions. Statute sets the class.
A college that awards associate's, bachelor's or master's degrees and few doctorates. NSF uses the class for its RUI and ROA opportunities.
A college or university that holds land-grant status under federal laws of 1862, 1890 or 1994. The status opens NIFA capacity funding and programmes reserved for each group.
A university that the Carnegie Classification places among Doctoral Universities with Very High Research Activity. Some programmes are open only to institutions outside that group.

term: Title III and Title V eligibility
short: A yearly Department of Education designation of colleges that enrol many needy students and spend little per student. Certain Higher Education Act grant programmes require it.
A lender certified by the Treasury's CDFI Fund to lend and invest in its community. Certification is the gate to the Fund's Financial Assistance awards.
A tax-exempt charity that falls outside the tax code's categories of public charity. It files a public return, Form 990-PF, every year.
A kind label on this guide's funder records for a private foundation that is not a company's, a community's or an operating foundation.
A kind label on four of this guide's funder records. In law a family foundation is a private foundation like any other.
A grantmaking public charity that serves one local area. Part of what it pays out follows the advice of its donors and is not open to application.
A private foundation whose assets come mainly from a for-profit company. A corporate giving programme is a different thing: it is run inside the company and files no public return of its own.
A private foundation that devotes most of its resources to carrying out its own charitable activities. The tax on failing to pay out a minimum amount does not apply to it.
A separately identified fund held by a sponsoring charity. The sponsor has legal control of the money, and the donor keeps the right to advise where grants go.
A charity that counts as a public charity because of its relationship to one or more other public charities that it supports.
A public charity whose main purpose is medical research and which carries that research out itself, in conjunction with a hospital.
The annual return every private foundation files with the IRS. It is public and shows the foundation's assets, every grant paid, and whether it takes unsolicited requests.
The annual return a tax-exempt organisation files with the IRS. Small organisations file the shorter Form 990-EZ or the electronic notice Form 990-N.
An identifying number the IRS issues to an organisation. A new organisation obtains one before it applies for tax exemption, and its filings are looked up by it.
The amount a grantmaking private foundation must pay out for charitable purposes each year, worked out from 5 percent of its investment assets.
A short first request to a foundation. The foundation reads it and then invites a full proposal from some of those who sent one.
A foundation's rule that it takes proposals only from organisations it has itself approached. A proposal sent without an invitation is not accepted.
A dated competition that a foundation opens to organisations it has not approached, with its own page, deadline and eligibility rule.
A rule under which a person cannot apply directly for an award: the institution puts the candidate forward, and the funder caps how many it may name.
A request for money that the funder did not invite. A private foundation states on its annual return whether it accepts such requests.
A grant that pays for an organisation's work as a whole and is not tied to one project.
A foundation grant that pays for one named piece of work with its own budget, as distinct from support for the organisation as a whole.
The application an organisation files with the IRS to be recognised as tax-exempt under section 501(c)(3). Form 1023-EZ is a shorter version open only to small organisations.
The letter in which the IRS says it has recognised an organisation as tax-exempt. Funders look it up to check a non-profit's standing.
Loss of tax-exempt status that follows of itself when an organisation files no annual return or notice for three years in a row.
An IRS letter to a central organisation that also recognises the organisations under its supervision as tax-exempt, so that they do not apply one by one.
The steps a private foundation must take when it funds an organisation that is not a public charity, to see that the grant is spent for its purpose and to report on it to the IRS.
A draft regulation that an agency publishes in the Federal Register for public comment. It applies to no one until a final rule is published and takes effect.
A regulation in its adopted form, published in the Federal Register with the date on which it takes effect.
A numbered presidential order that directs federal agencies, published in the Federal Register. It tells agencies what to do and does not itself rewrite a regulation.
A court order that bars an agency from carrying out or enforcing a policy or action. It protects the parties the order names.
A court's cancelling of an agency policy, notice or decision, so that it is no longer in effect. Court orders also say that the action is set aside.
The state of a court ruling that a party has taken to a higher court. The ruling may stay in force or be paused, by a stay, while the appeal runs.
A law in which Congress provides money to federal agencies for a fiscal year. It can also carry conditions on how grant money is used.
A stopgap law that keeps agencies funded at a set rate for a limited time when a fiscal year starts without full-year appropriations.
What the President asks Congress to provide for an agency in the coming fiscal year. It is a proposal; the amounts are set by the appropriations acts.
The cancelling of something already in place. Congress rescinds money it had appropriated; an agency rescinds a notice or an award term it had issued.
This guide's label for a change that has been signed, announced or enacted but has not yet taken effect or been carried out in full.
The one-word label this guide puts on each programme record to say where its competition stood on the day the funder's pages were read.
This guide's label for a programme with no notice for the current cycle and no statement from the funder that it has ended. It reports an absence, not a closure.
This guide's label for a programme whose funder has said that the competition is cancelled, paused or will not be held.
